lines.trans: Relax, my friend, do not be so nervous.
He simply wants to get a rise out of me.
Do not take offense at my words.
What do you want to tell me?
She would never choose you.
Why are you so confident about this?
She is a beautiful and mature woman.
And you are simply a broke young cook.
I know her from a completely different side.
Do you want to drink some juice with me?
No, thank you, I am at work right now.
Well, suit yourself, it is your business.
I will still talk with her anyway.

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'and', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('so, and what about') (starting a question: а жвачку?) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: Qualitative or relational adjective formed with the productive '-н-' suffix, meaning 'poor' and agreeing in gender, number, and case.
Secondary conversational sense ('poor') (pitiful: бедный мальчик = poor boy) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Я ухожу. Ваш сын будет бедным и честным.
examples.trans: I'm leaving. Your son will be poor and honest.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'in' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('into, to') (+ accusative (where to)) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('all') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.
Secondary conversational sense ('everything') (neuter всё) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('everyone') (plural все) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

взрослый.gloss: adult, grown-up; (as a noun) a grown-up

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'adult', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.
as a noun, often plural: взрослые = grown-ups

examples.text: Маленькие умеют терпеть, а взрослые нет, понял?
examples.trans: Little ones can hold on, but grown-ups can't, got it?

meanings.en: to choose, select; to use up completely (quotas, limits)
meanings.note: Prefix 'вы-' ('out of') marks outward movement or thorough completion (stem 'брать'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to choose', forming an aspectual pair with 'выбирать'.

examples.text: В этом году все квоты выбрали.
examples.trans: This year all the quotas have been used up.
She chose the most beautiful dress.
Agreed, I will choose a movie.

выпить.gloss: to drink, to have a drink

meanings.en: to drink up, to have a drink
meanings.note: often used without an object for drinking alcohol

examples.trans: Oh, I've had a bit to drink now.
May I drink a tiny drop of beer?

meanings.note: Declinable neuter noun meaning 'matter', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('matter, business') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('case (in court)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I have a lot to do.

examples.text: Мне некогда об этом думать. Слишком много дел.
examples.trans: I have no time to think about that. There's too much to do.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'friend' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: This is Vanya, my childhood friend.

examples.text: Это Паша, мой заместитель. Это Ваня, друг моего детства.
examples.trans: This is Pasha, my deputy. This is Vanya, my childhood friend.

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('other, another, different').
Secondary conversational sense ('different') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Послушайте, а можно в другое место? Здесь плохо пахнет.
examples.trans: Listen, could we go somewhere else? It smells bad in here.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'woman' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Твоя жена очень мудрая женщина. Ты её слушай.
examples.trans: Your wife is a very wise woman. You listen to her.

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to know'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: emphasis: вот поэтому ты и... = that's exactly why you...

examples.trans: I was born and grew up here.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'how'.
Secondary conversational sense ('as') (как вы знаете = as you know) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('beautiful, handsome').

examples.trans: They have a very beautiful house.

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('my') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.
молодой человек = young man (polite address)

examples.text: Молодой человек, как на тест-драйв записаться?
examples.trans: Young man, how do I sign up for a test drive?

examples.text: Молодой человек, а как на тест-драйв записаться?
examples.trans: Young man, how do I sign up for a test drive?

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'on' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('onto, to; for') (+ accusative: на второй срок) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: The programme is on the website.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: goes right before the word it negates

Negative prefix 'не-' ('un-, non-, not') (stem 'рвничать'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to be nervous', forming an aspectual pair with 'разнервничаться'.

examples.trans: Don't be nervous, everything is fine.

examples.text: Павел Юрьевич, вам нельзя нервничать сейчас.
examples.trans: Pavel Yuryevich, you mustn't get worked up right now.

meanings.note: + genitive: 'у нас нет выбора' = we have no choice
Secondary conversational sense ('there isn't') (+ genitive) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
used with не before the verb, or alone

examples.text: Я никогда не был на море.
examples.trans: I've never been to the sea.

examples.text: Я никогда в жизни не пробовал такой вкусной утки!
examples.trans: I have never in my life tasted such delicious duck!

meanings.note: hesitation, at the start of a sentence
Secondary conversational sense ('oh come on!') (ну, папа!) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.

обижаться.gloss: to take offence, to be hurt

meanings.en: to take offence, to get upset
meanings.note: Prefix 'об-' ('around, about') marks encirclement or comprehensive action (stem 'ижаться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to take offence, to be hurt', paired with 'обидеться'.

examples.trans: Don't be offended by my words.

examples.text: Да не обижайся ты, Ваня. Сейчас найду подходящую одежду.
examples.trans: Don't take offence, Vanya. I'll find suitable clothes right now.

meanings.note: accusative/genitive его (него after prepositions), dative ему (нему)
Secondary conversational sense ('it') (for masculine and neuter things) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
High-frequency Russian pronoun ('she') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.

examples.text: Паша, я больше не хочу о ней слышать. Понял?
examples.trans: Pasha, I don't want to hear about her again. Understood?

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'cook', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: Есть такой английский повар. Я по его передачам научусь готовить.
examples.trans: There is this English chef. I will learn to cook from his shows.

examples.text: Я хочу работать поваром в ресторане.
examples.trans: I want to work as a cook in a restaurant.

meanings.en: to have a talk, to speak (with someone)
meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'говорить'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to have a talk', forming an aspectual pair with 'говорить'.

examples.text: Поговори с Аракеляном. Пусть он заберёт заявление.
examples.trans: Talk to Arakelyan. Get him to withdraw his statement.

позлить.gloss: to anger, to tease, to annoy

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'злить'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to anger', forming an aspectual pair with 'злить'.

examples.text: Он просто хотел немного позлить своего друга.
examples.trans: He simply wanted to tease his friend a little.
He simply wants to get a rise out of me.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'why'.

examples.trans: Why are we going so slowly?

examples.text: Виталик, почему мы так медленно едем? Быстрее!
examples.trans: Vitalik, why are we going so slowly? Faster!

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'just'.
Secondary conversational sense ('easy') (это просто = it's easy) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Мы просто не хотели вас беспокоить. Всё отменим!
examples.trans: We just didn't want to bother you. We'll cancel it all!

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'work', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('job') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
almost always in 'всё равно' = it doesn't matter; мне всё равно = I don't care

examples.text: Мне всё равно. Что ты, что он.
examples.trans: It's all the same to me. You or him.

meanings.note: Prefix 'рас-' ('apart, un-, thoroughly') indicates distribution or intensive action (stem 'слабиться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to relax', paired with 'расслабляться'.

examples.text: Ваня, расслабься. В этот раз без обмана.
examples.trans: Vanya, relax. This time there's no trick.

meanings.note: + instrumental; со before some consonant clusters: со всеми

examples.trans: Share it all equally with everyone, understand?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'даваться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to give up, to surrender', paired with 'сдаться'.

examples.text: Никогда не сдавайся! Сегодня я выйду отсюда под подписку!
examples.trans: Never give up! Today I'm getting out of here on a travel ban!

meanings.note: 'сейчас буду' = I'll be right there
Secondary conversational sense ('in a moment') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Конечно, помогу. Кто у вас сейчас начальник?
examples.trans: Of course I'll help. Who's your boss now?

meanings.note: once; что скажешь? = what do you say?
Secondary conversational sense ('tell me / tell us') (polite request) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Tell us, when will your programme be out?

meanings.note: 'дать слово' = to give one's word, 'держать слово' = to keep one's word
'дать слово' = to give one's word, 'держать слово' = to keep one's word

examples.text: А что я за мэр такой, который держит своё слово?
examples.trans: And what kind of mayor would I be if I kept my word?

собираться.gloss: to intend, to be about to; to gather

meanings.en: to intend, to plan, to be going to
meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'обираться'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to intend', forming an aspectual pair with 'собраться'. The reflexive suffix '-ся'/'-сь' makes the action intransitive, reciprocal, or directed at the subject.
Secondary conversational sense ('to gather, to get ready') (pack or assemble) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Ну и что? Я всё равно переезжать собираюсь.
examples.trans: So what? I'm planning to move anyway.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'quite'.
Secondary conversational sense ('not at all') (совсем не) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Я совсем не это хочу сказать.
examples.trans: That's not what I mean at all.

examples.text: Нет, Вика, я совсем не это хочу сказать.
examples.trans: No, Vika, that's not what I mean at all.

meanings.note: Formed with a diminutive/expressive Slavic suffix adding warmth or small scale. Common masculine noun meaning 'juice' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: I will drink a little good juice.
Make me some fresh orange juice.

meanings.note: спасибо за + accusative = thank you for

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: с другой стороны = on the other hand
Secondary conversational sense ('direction') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: On the other hand, it's interesting.
The shop is on that side.

examples.text: Бред какой-то. Но, с другой стороны, чем я рискую?
examples.trans: What nonsense. But on the other hand, what have I got to lose?

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('so') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or discourse tone in spoken dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('like that, so') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: So I shouldn't wait for you?
So I shouldn't wait for you tonight?

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('your') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.

examples.text: Я бы на твоём месте подумал.
examples.trans: If I were you, I'd think about it.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('you') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: Qualitative or relational adjective formed with the productive '-н-' suffix, meaning 'confident' and agreeing in gender, number, and case.
Secondary conversational sense ('sure, certain') (short form уверен / уверена) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Что-то голос какой-то не очень уверенный.
examples.trans: Your voice doesn't sound very confident.
He answered in a calm, confident voice.

examples.text: Что-то голос какой-то не очень уверенный. Что конкретно?
examples.trans: Your voice doesn't sound very confident. What specifically?

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to want', forming an aspectual pair with 'захотеть'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.trans: If you don't want to, suit yourself.
They want to build a shopping centre there.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('what') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('that') (conjunction) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('? = well?') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: pointing at a thing or a situation; 'это' + noun = 'this is ...'
points at something: это моё = that's mine
Secondary conversational sense ('is') (linking word: главное — это народ) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: And this is for you. A toy car!

meanings.note: меня = me (genitive/accusative), мне = to me (dative)
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
